title: 5 winners and 5 losers from the Bahrain GP in Malaysia
excerpt:
Max Verstappen returned to winning ways with a beautiful drive at a rain-hit Sepang, in a race that featured plenty of overtaking. But while he and his Red Bull team celebrated, many of his rivals were left downbeat. Lawrence Barretto selects his winners and losers from the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Winner: Max Verstappen

Verstappen kicked off the event on the front foot with some impressive pace in Friday practice. He carried that into the weekend, taking his 49th pole position and first of the season. It was the first time a non-Mercedes powered car started in P1 in 2026.

title: How McLaren got their sums wrong on Sepang tyre strategy
excerpt:
Just eight days after the team failed to score any points in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, McLaren endured another painful race day at Sepang.

It wasn’t quite as bad as Baku, but nevertheless P6 for Oscar Piastri and P9 for Lando Norris was not what the team needs or expects.

On a day when there were many strategy calls to be made, the team got the big one wrong when they opted to put both drivers on medium tyres for the start – a decision that seemed logical at the time but which was soon proved to be incorrect.

Historically Sepang is a track that dries relatively quickly, and thanks to its rough surface, puts heat into dry tyres and allows them to work even in damp conditions. That knowledge pushed McLaren and others into starting on slicks.

“At the pit wall, in terms of making calls and strategy on tyres, the most difficult moment was certainly at the start,” Team Principal Andrea Stella noted. “Where it wasn't clear [was] whether the track was requiring intermediate tyres, or it would work for the dry tyres.

“On this kind of tarmac already what we saw on the laps to the grid is that the intermediate tyres were getting damaged very rapidly, and also on this kind of tarmac, the dry tyres work very, very easily – much more easily than pretty much every other circuit.

“So it looked, from what we could observe, that the track was dry enough to stay on track with the dry tyres, and we thought that the dry tyres would have switched on pretty rapidly. But as a matter of fact, it took more laps than we thought.

“So with Lando we lost race time, and with Oscar as well, we lost race time because we needed to pit and accept that the track was only right for intermediate tyres. This was the most complicated moment.”

Piastri made a decisive call and pitted for intermediates at the end of the second formation lap, throwing away his grid position but at least putting himself on the right tyres.

The slick runners struggled so much that by the end of the first flying lap he was already back up to P10, just four spots shy of his starting position. Norris, meanwhile, had soon tumbled down to P15, and like the others still on dry tyres he lost huge chunks of time each lap.

McLaren were one of several teams where one driver pitted, and the other stuck with the slicks. However, that wasn’t a big picture choice.

“No, it wasn't as simple as splitting,” said Stella. “It was more the uncertainty as to how much it would take for the dry tyres to start to work, and as a matter of fact, it took longer than what we thought it would take.

“So ultimately, it was an incorrect judgment as to the crossover at which the dry tyres would be faster than the intermediate tyres. But there was not a logic as simple as saying, ‘Let's split, and let's see what which one is right.’ We thought that the dry tyres would switch on faster.”

Piastri admits McLaren 'need to improve' after Malaysia P6

The drivers had their input, as Stella confirmed: “I think for Oscar it was sort of Oscar himself thinking like it's not going to be rapid, and I think with Lando, it's possible that we biased Lando in the wrong direction.

“I think he was probably more in the direction that he should have pitted for inters, but as we discussed, we kind of attempted to see whether we could stay out on the medium tyres.”

By the last Safety Car, Piastri and Norris had made it up P7 and P8. George Russell’s late retirement handed the Australian a place, but Norris was wrongfooted when the Safety Car queue backed up, and he dropped to P11. After the restart he managed to gain a couple of places.

McLaren did thus at least score some points, but this was by no means a good weekend for a team that was winning races just a few weeks ago.

“We see a scenario in F1 which seems to be changing pretty rapidly,” said Stella. “In Hungary, we took some upgrades, and we were in condition to have pole position in Hungary, Zandvoort, and then we were in condition to do pole position and pretty much victory in Madrid without the Virtual Safety Car.

“And then very rapidly and interestingly, as we took upgrades as well, the picture changes. I think we have to take a look at our own development.

“We don't see any anomaly in our data, but we have to acknowledge that potentially some competitors have developed their car with bigger steps that we did.”

Stella admitted that the pecking order is hard to judge at the moment, especially after a race an outlying track like Sepang. He reserved judgement on what we might see in Singapore next weekend.

“It's a very special condition here in Malaysia,” he said. “So I think we'll have to understand better the behaviour of the cars, and also here Ferrari were very, very strong.

“I think you see that [Lewis] Hamilton was out there with Lando, and from that position he managed to recover several positions, overtaking cars through the race, meaning that it was definitely one of the best cars out there.

“I think we need to give ourselves some more time. I'm personally not in condition to say if Singapore will be now more suitable or not, because from a track layout point of view, we thought that here would be a decent circuit for us, and this because of the uncertainty caused by the new scenario from a competitiveness point of view, but also because we might have to understand a bit better the upgrades that we took ourselves. And Singapore will give us a better answer.”

title: Audi unveil special livery for Singapore GP
excerpt:
Audi have revealed a special livery for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, celebrating the city's unique identity as well as the team's first night race in Formula 1.

The R26 will sport a design that combines a Singapore-specific variant of Audi's usual Titanium Silver Grey with a traditional peranakan pattern, which will adorn the sidepods and rear wing and carry over onto Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto's race suits.

Inspired by the city's transition from daylight to twilight, the livery has been launched alongside a limited-edition Adidas capsule collection, building on 'The Art of Influence' – a 360-degree programme that brings F1 closer to fans through activations across Singapore and online.

Stefano Battiston, Chief Brand and Commercial Officer at Audi, said: “Bringing Formula 1 to the people means giving fans more ways to feel part of the team, wherever they are. Singapore shows how we can do that through one connected idea.

"Audi’s special livery expresses our brand through a design shaped by the city, and fans around the world can discover it for themselves through the online reveal.

"With the Adidas collection and experiences across Singapore, that story continues beyond the race car.

"‘The Art of Influence’ invites people to engage with the team in ways that are meaningful to them, whether they are here in the city or following from home."

title: Vasseur on how Hamilton and Leclerc saved the day at Sepang
excerpt:
Ferrari weren’t the only team to make a wrong call at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia by opting for slicks, but no one else did a better job of recovering and limiting the damage.

A race that looked to be heading for disaster after just a couple of laps ended with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc recovering for a decent outcome to finish third and fourth.

Yes, they were flattered by the late retirement of George Russell moving them both up a spot, while Isack Hadjar was hampered by a late battery issue and thus was unable to put up much of a defence.

But they did most of the work themselves with some superb driving in what was clearly a very competitive package – a performance that inevitably left Ferrari fans wondering what might have been had the right call been made at the start.

“I think 50 percent of the cars went for slicks, 50 for wets,” said Team Principal Fred Vasseur of the tyre choice. “You can't try, you just have a look on the tarmac in front of you in the pit lane, and for sure it was not the good one.

“It's not that I have no regrets – for sure, it's clear that it was better to start with inters, but we did the choice with information that we had.”

In essence the track dried more slowly than anyone expected, given past experience of Sepang.

“When you have to take your decision, you are trying to base the decision on good parameters,” said Vasseur. “But for sure, at the end of the day, we have to be lucid that it was not the right call, that it would have been much better for us to start with inters. But we were considering that it will dry very quickly, and so on. The pit stop [loss] was quite long also, 26 seconds.”

Leclerc’s race was changed when he had contact with Nico Hulkenberg at the start, and he pitted immediately for inters and a new front wing.

Several drivers who went for slicks also soon abandoned them – in some cases even before the first flying lap – but Hamilton opted to stay out, insisting that it was right to take a risk.

“We let him [have] the choice,” said Vasseur. “At the end, in this situation, they are in the car. When we are telling him that we are ready, it's just to tell him that he can pit if he thinks that it's the right call.

“He did a very good race, very smooth strategy. He was able to do a mega long stint with a very good tyre management with the soft.”

So what was the potential had the Ferraris made a different call and started on intermediates?

“I don't know, because the race is for sure different when you have to overtake 20 cars rather than run in front,” said Vasseur. “But I was not mega optimistic after Lap 1! You never know also because with dirty air, it's much more difficult, energy management and so on.

“But the pace was solid, and when Lewis was at the end of his stint with the soft, he was still doing a very good lap time.”

The race pace was certainly impressive, and ultimately that’s what propelled Hamilton and Leclerc up the order.

“We showed the same pace yesterday,” said Vasseur. “We were on the first row, but we were also on the first row in Baku. But the race pace was much better this weekend.

“It's also completely different conditions. The last two or three races we had zero [degradation]. This weekend the race was also difficult to manage for the drivers, because we did all the free practice with 60 degrees of track temp, and then you do the race with 30 degrees less, and it's another track.

“We were all a bit lost. I think when we restarted after the Safety Car, at one stage you had seven cars with soft, seven with medium, seven with hard. It's not very usual.”

So can Ferrari carry that strong form into next weekend?

“Let me have a beer tonight, and we discuss about Singapore tomorrow morning!” joked Vasseur. “It will be another one, for sure. But each one is different, and let's see.

“We were expecting to do a good performance this weekend. I think we did it. We are expecting to do also a good one next week – and I hope we'll do it.”

title: Lindblad's P10 finish 'more than we could have imagined'
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad believes his P10 finish at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was "more than we could have ever imagined" after starting from the back of the grid.

The Racing Bulls driver started Sunday's 55-lap race at the Sepang International Circuit in P22 and last on the grid after taking grid penalties for new engine components.

Lindblad was able to move up the field early in proceedings after starting on the intermediate tyre, as other drivers dropped away with slick tyres on the still-wet track.

A late retirement for Mercedes' George Russell and an off-track excursion for Lando Norris' McLaren behind the Safety Car ensured the 19-year-old scored his fourth points finish in succession.

"It's probably the busiest day of my F1 career and the outcome is pretty amazing. To be in the points from starting last is more than we could have ever imagined," said Lindblad, who is still in his rookie F1 season.

"I think from that side it's really good, amazing day for the team, amazing day for the whole Red Bull family, credit to Max [Verstappen] and RBPT. It's the first win for this engine, it's been absolutely amazing all year so I'm super happy for them.

"On my side, I'm not that happy with my own performance. Obviously there was some good stuff but there was a good part in the middle where I was just too slow, so I need to understand why and why I've been a little bit weaker I'd say in long runs than short runs this year.

"I've always felt good in Qualifying but the race is normally a bit more difficult, so I need to understand why that is, but super happy for the team. They've all done an absolutely perfect job, it's honestly thanks to them that we've got this performance today."

Racing Bulls enjoyed a strong day in Malaysia, as Liam Lawson finished seventh, having even battled eventual race winner Max Verstappen for third on the opening lap after an incredible launch off the grid from P11.

The result means Racing Bulls has moved 22 points clear of Alpine in their battle for P5 in the Teams' Championship, as neither Pierre Gasly or Franco Colapinto scored points in Malaysia.

"It's sort of two weekends where Alpine has been a bit quicker than us but we've managed to out-score them," said Lawson.

"I think that's really been on good decision making today on the strategy for the start. I had one of the best starts I've ever had in my career and that put us in a great position for the rest of the race."

title: How Alonso and Aston Martin took their opportunity in Sepang
excerpt:
Despite his P12 starting position, Fernando Alonso was sceptical about his prospects of finishing in the points ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The Spaniard’s theory was that he would be vulnerable on the straights in the early laps, and then would not have the pace with which to regain any lost places.

However, rain on an eventful Sunday in Sepang upset his predictions and he ended the race in P8 – despite making the wrong tyre call for the start of a Grand Prix that had a few surprises in store.

Both Aston Martin drivers have retired on a regular basis in 2026, and Alonso mischievously suggested that it wasn’t fair that there was a grid reset after several drivers experienced problems on the original formation lap, noting that “I think I had 50 per cent DNFs this year. They never stopped the race for us. Yeah, that was quite strange!”

When the race eventually got underway the track was wet but drying, and in common with McLaren, Ferrari, Alpine, Audi, Cadillac and Haas (with one car), Aston opted for slicks, in this case mediums.

“The rain was very much appreciated in terms of opportunities for us,” said Alonso. “And we even started with slicks because we thought that the rain was not anymore there. It took quite long to restart the race, but I'm sure there is an explanation.”

All the drivers who went for slicks soon found it was a bad choice. But while his team mate Lance Stroll quickly abandoned them and switched to intermediates, Alonso joined the group who stayed out, essentially hoping that a Safety Car would allow a cheap tyre changed and close up the field.

Remarkably he even passed his former McLaren team mate Lewis Hamilton as they slithered around and looked for grip.

In the end the hoped-for Safety Car came, and after the resumption Alonso made steady progress up the order. He made it into the points when he passed Arvid Lindblad just before the late VSC that turned into the second full Safety Car period.

Subsequently a retirement for George Russell and a mishap for Lando Norris promoted Alonso to P8, and after the restart he stayed there – safely in front of Norris – for the run to the flag.

An Aston Martin holding off the World Champion and a double 2026 race winner was likely not on anyone’s Sepang bingo card…

“I think it is the track,” said Alonso. “I think we've been more competitive this weekend in general, both cars in Q2, and today fighting in the midfield territory. So yeah, overall it was a better weekend. Let's see if we can keep up this pace, especially in Singapore, where we have some hopes next weekend.

“And then there are some other weeks that we are very uncompetitive, and we have to accept it. The weekends that we can score points, the important thing is to execute well the race. Today, obviously, we started with a slick, so we put ourselves in some difficulties there – but at the end it was it was okay. After the Safety Car, we had a new race coming.”

Aston Martin's Chief Trackside Officer Mike Krack admitted that the team had simply got it wrong with the tyre choice.

"I think we did some good decisions, but we did also some that were less good, and this we need to review clearly,” he said. “We then bailed out [of the slicks] with Lance, with Fernando we continued. We were just in the debrief, and he said it didn't feel that bad until the intermediate runners came and just flew by.

“But clearly that's something we need to go through. Yes it was hot, and yes it was drying, but we saw that 50 per cent of the field did what we did, but 50 per cent did not get it right. So that's something we need to clearly have a look at.”

Things then turned in the team’s favour: “I think we were fortunate with the Safety Car to close up again, and then it started more going into a normal race. I think it was quite intense, quite interesting. A lot happened.

“A good end at the end of the day, with a lot of incidents that were probably masking here and there. But I said it this morning, opportunities, if they come, we don't have the pace to finish in the points on a regular basis yet. So we need to grab opportunity, and I think that is what we did today.”

Despite the result Krack wasn’t getting too excited, while acknowledging that it was encouraging for a team that has faced such a difficult time this season.

“I think, let's not forget, three weeks ago we were in Madrid, one week ago we were in Baku, and we were just nowhere,” he said. “I think we need to keep our feet on the ground here, analyse really why we were more competitive here, and look ahead and see how we can benefit more from that.

“To be honest for the team it's great, because we have been really through tough times, and the few positive moments that you get you have to – I'm not saying celebrate like a World Championship party – but I think you need to take a breath and acknowledge when good results come your way, because we have not been fortunate enough to have many.”

title: Mekies on why Verstappen’s victory meant so much to Red Bull
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies has praised Max Verstappen’s “outstanding” performance in the Bahrain Grand Prix that earned Red Bull their first victory of the 2026 season, marking a “milestone moment in the history” of the team.

At the start of the year Red Bull were significantly off the pace set by Mercedes, but their various upgrade packages since helped them to close the gap and eventually fulfil their ambition of returning to the top step of the podium.

A week after he missed out on winning the Azerbaijan Grand Prix by just 0.196s, Verstappen dominated Qualifying in Malaysia to take pole position. He lost out to his Mercedes rivals in the race's early laps before charging back through to seal a long-awaited triumph over Kimi Antonelli and Lewis Hamilton.

The result was made even more special as it represented Red Bull’s first win since they switched to producing their own power units in partnership with Ford, giving them their first taste of success since Honda departed the project.

"This is another milestone moment in the history of this team: the first victory for us as a power unit manufacturer with Red Bull Ford Powertrains in its very first season,” Mekies reflected.

“The credit goes to all the people involved who have been working incredibly hard on this project over the past five years. Everyone in Milton Keynes and at the track deserves this moment and should celebrate it as an important step towards many more victories in the future.

"The first win of the season is a great way to finish what has been an extremely successful weekend overall. After showing strong pace in every session and securing our first pole position of the season [on Saturday], Max converted that performance into an outstanding P1.

“In often chaotic circumstances, he remained in control throughout the race, managed the conditions brilliantly, showed the strongest pace and delivered exactly the kind of performance we know he is capable of.

"More broadly, this result confirms the progress we have been making in recent months. We were already close several times, and today we converted that pace. The team has been working tirelessly to improve our package, and weekends like this are the reward for that effort.”

For a large part of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, it looked like Red Bull could secure consecutive double podiums as Isack Hadjar brought himself back into contention after starting in eighth place, but a battery issue restricted him to fifth.

Mekies explained: "There are naturally mixed feelings on the other side of the garage because Isack also showed very strong pace all weekend. We could have rounded off this weekend with another double podium; unfortunately, not everything went well with his car.

“Finishing fifth still represents a strong result considering where he started, but naturally it is frustrating when you know more was possible. We will analyse exactly what happened, take the positives from a weekend where both drivers were consistently competitive, and immediately turn our focus to Singapore.

"However, everyone should enjoy a well-deserved victory and an important milestone for this team."

title: Piastri admits McLaren ‘need to improve’ after Malaysia P6
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri believes that McLaren “need to improve” after his P6 result at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, with the Australian stating that the team “just weren’t quick enough” to keep up with some of their rivals.

In an eventful afternoon at the Sepang International Circuit, Piastri and team mate Lando Norris were amongst a small group to bolt on the medium tyres for the start of the race – which had been delayed due to heavy rainfall.

The choice proved to be the wrong one, with the track still not dry enough for slicks when the event got underway. Piastri subsequently pitted at the end of the first lap to switch to the intermediates, dropping him backwards through the field.

After working his way forwards again – and making a second pit stop under the first Safety Car for the hard tyres – Piastri narrowly escaped being collected by Norris as the Briton ran off track during the last Safety Car phase later on.

Ultimately the driver from Melbourne came home in sixth place – the same position in which he had started – and spoke positively about his own performance in the race, whilst also acknowledging that there were some areas for improvement.

“Overall, reasonably happy,” said Piastri afterwards. “I think it went pretty well on a personal note. I felt like I did a pretty good job today, which was good. Unfortunately we just weren't quick enough to really do that much.

“The last Safety Car was a bit of a shame, because I was catching Charles [Leclerc] pretty quick. But no, apart from that, just a tricky afternoon. We didn't quite make the right calls, and ultimately we weren't quick enough, so that was the biggest thing.”

When asked whether it feels like McLaren are now behind the likes of Mercedes, Ferrari and Red Bull in terms of pace, Piastri responded: “Yeah, I mean, I think Red Bull clearly here have been incredibly fast, for sure. I think it's been the strongest they've been.

“I think clearly whatever they put on the car in Baku's been a big step forward for them, because last weekend without the bad Qualifying they had, they probably would have… well, I mean Max [Verstappen] nearly won the race anyway, and this weekend Max did win the race, so they've been very, very strong the last couple of weekends.

“I think us and Ferrari seem a little bit in a similar ballpark, but that ballpark is not fighting for race wins, so we need to improve. We know that, and we'll try our best to make sure we try and improve.”

title: All the key moments from the 2026 Bahrain GP in Malaysia
excerpt:
The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia delivered an action-packed weekend, culminating in Max Verstappen reaching the top step of the podium for the first time in 2026.

There were also plenty of other talking points that emerged across the three days of action, from George Russell’s dramatic retirement to the Sepang International Circuit staging a thriller on its return to F1.

Here are all the key moments from the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia…

Verstappen and Red Bull get back to winning ways

Red Bull took on a huge challenge in the build-up to F1’s all-new 2026 regulations by investing in their own power unit facility and creating an engine from the ground up.

With that in mind, Verstappen and team mate Isack Hadjar’s combined tally of nine Grand Prix podium finishes across the first 15 rounds of the season was rather impressive – plenty of promise being shown, even if reliability caused a few headaches.

Verstappen and Red Bull are winners, though, and podiums were not going to satisfy them for much longer.

After coming within two tenths of victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, the Dutchman and his team continued their positive momentum into the Sepang weekend, where Verstappen triumphed on F1’s last visit to the Malaysian venue back in 2017.

Using plenty of lessons from the first half of the season, and boosted by recent updates, Verstappen charged to a breakthrough 2026 pole position on Saturday – lapping almost three tenths quicker than nearest challenger Lewis Hamilton.

While Sunday threw everything at the drivers, including heavy rain, suspended starts, delays, mixed conditions, Safety Car restarts and more, nothing could stop the four-time World Champion from converting that pole into the race win.

It might have come too late for a championship comeback this year, but underlines that Verstappen and Red Bull are a force to be reckoned with once more, and should head into 2027 as serious contenders.

Verstappen 'incredibly proud' after historic Bahrain GP win

Mixed fortunes for Mercedes as the title battle takes a big turn

There were contrasting fortunes for the two Mercedes drivers in Sepang. Kimi Antonelli grabbed a podium to extend his lead in the championship, and while it was not the win, second place on a day where treacherous conditions could have derailed his title charge was a very strong result, but one that the team would likely describe as bittersweet.

That is because George Russell failed to finish, his power unit giving up the ghost with only a handful of laps to go. Prior to this the Briton had struggled to match his team mate in Malaysia, despite getting past Antonelli early on.

He could not hold the Italian at bay once Antonelli got his tyres up to temperature, and was unable to stick with the youngster despite him at one point running wide and collecting a bollard.

But Russell was on for a solid P3 and thus would have only lost a further three points to Antonelli in the title fight. His DNF means the gap between the two now stands at 84 points, or over three Grand Prix victories.

Russell’s DNF was not the only disappointment for the team, with the first big upgrade package bolted onto the car since Canada not having the desired effect. Mercedes struggled for pace with respect to Red Bull across the weekend as a whole, and could not get that set-up into the sweet spot.

They have work to do to understand those updates before Singapore next weekend, but in Antonelli they do have a driver in fine form, who was able to put his mistakes from Baku firmly behind him and deliver the sort of performance that has taken him to such a commanding lead in the standings.

Superb recovery drives as Ferrari fail to nail strategy calls

Ferrari were not the only team caught out by the track conditions, but their decision to fit both cars with soft tyres when the race got underway nearly proved their undoing. On a wet track, Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc plummeted down the order, the latter’s day made worse with contact that forced an early pit stop.

Hamilton deserves credit for holding his nerve, staying out on the softs as others realised their mistake and pitted for intermediates, and getting the C4 rubber to work for him as conditions began to dry.

He climbed back up the order with a drive reminiscent of some of his very best from days gone by, and would likely have challenged for third even without the late Safety Car bunching up the field.

The seven-time World Champion recorded his first rostrum since Silverstone with that P3 finish, leading many to wonder what might have been had he started on the intermediates like the Red Bull and Mercedes drivers.

As for Leclerc, his recovery took longer after he found himself last thanks to that contact and subsequent pit stop. But he deserves equal credit for working hard to climb back into the top 10, a late move on Isack Hadjar bagging him P4 – the position he believes he would have finished in no matter what.

Leclerc relieved with P4 after everything went 'wrong' in Sepang

A hectic afternoon for McLaren

For McLaren it was an eventful race too, with both cars being amongst a small number to start on the slick medium tyres in still-wet conditions.

After initially falling back, Oscar Piastri pitted for intermediates at the end of the first lap while Lando Norris stayed out – something the Briton said after the race was a “gamble”.

When the track dried out, both drivers moved through the field, with the Australian winding up ahead of his team mate despite making an extra stop and not running on the clearly favoured soft tyre at any point.

There was a hairy moment for the McLaren pit wall when Norris nearly crashed into the back of Piastri as the cars ahead bunched up following George Russell’s retirement under the late Safety Car, with Norris running off track and dropping down the order as a result.

The reigning World Champion ultimately recovered to finish P9 – and later received a reprimand for driving erratically under Safety Car conditions – with Piastri taking the chequered flag in sixth place.

Alonso secures points for Aston Martin

Despite Fernando Alonso’s record of winning three times with three different teams in Sepang, before this weekend it seemed a long shot that he could bring his Aston Martin home in the points after the squad’s beleaguered season so far.

But the Spaniard did just that, finishing in eighth place, while team mate Lance Stroll was not far behind either in P12.

The AMR26 suddenly showed signs of promise when it hit the track in Malaysia, with both drivers getting into Q2 on merit and gaining a few grid places thanks to penalties around them.

Alonso started on medium tyres for Sunday’s race and dropped back, before pitting for the hard compound and running a long stint.

He managed to stay out of trouble, benefitted from other incidents, and had fresh softs for the end to fight with - holding on to deny Lando Norris by half a second to finish P8, his best result of the season, and bringing back some much-needed points for the Silverstone-based outfit.

While Stroll couldn’t quite match Alonso’s result, the Canadian later said that he had enjoyed being able to battle in the race and fight towards the points – something the Aston Martin drivers have not been able to say for some time.

Sepang delivers a thriller on its F1 return

As touched on earlier, F1 had not raced at Sepang for almost a decade when Malaysia agreed to step in and stage the Bahrain Grand Prix.

For the drivers who had previously experienced the venue, it was a welcome return, and for those who had not, there were plenty of smiles during Friday practice as they got to grips with a fast and flowing layout.

The hot, humid conditions understandably posed a challenge, as did the tyre degradation seen throughout FP1, FP2 and FP3 – leading to the prospect of a fascinating, strategic Grand Prix on Sunday.

The situation was flipped on its head when the heavens opened around an hour before the race start, though, soaking the track and setting up a race that started in damp conditions and transitioned to the dry.

On a chaotic afternoon, there was action from start to finish to keep the many thousands of passionate fans watching trackside on the edge of their seats, as Sepang delivered another F1 classic that will be remembered for years to come.

title: F2 and F3 unveil 2027 calendars racing across four continents
excerpt:
Formula 2 has confirmed its 2027 calendar, with 14 rounds spanning Asia, Oceania, Europe and the Americas.

Istanbul and Mexico City join the schedule as new venues, both staged in October, while Montreal returns following its addition to the 2026 campaign.

The season opens in Sakhir in March alongside Formula 1, before a direct trip to Jeddah a week later. The field then heads to Melbourne and on to Montreal.

The European leg begins at Monte-Carlo in June, followed by a Silverstone and Spielberg double-header in July ahead of the summer break. September brings three rounds in succession: Monza, Madrid and Baku.

October sees F2 race at Istanbul for the first time, at the demanding circuit returning to the F1 calendar, before heading to Mexico City for another new addition. The season closes with back-to-back finales in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in December.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said the calendar "reflects the continued strength and global growth of an important championship at the heart of our driver development pathway."

He added: "The addition of Istanbul and Mexico City will bring Formula 2 to new audiences and give the next generation of talent the opportunity to compete on an even greater variety of circuits around the world."

Formula 1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali said the calendar "will deliver another exciting season of racing across 14 rounds at some of the most iconic and challenging venues in world motorsport."

"Formula 2 continues to play a vital role as the ultimate pathway to Formula 1," he said.

F3 has also unveiled its calendar and will race in 10 rounds, from Bahrain and Jeddah in March, through to Turkey in early October, taking in Melbourne, Montreal, Monaco, Silverstone, Austria, Monza and Madrid along the way.

Verstappen's extended Red Bull contract, running through 2030, gives him a potential runway of at least four more full seasons to close the gap, assuming the team can maintain competitiveness through the new technical regulations.

After breaking its win drought in Sepang, can Red Bull build on that and keep delivering winning machinery into next year and beyond, one that will shape Verstappen's realistic chances of reaching 91 wins, let alone surpassing them, before his contract expires?

title: Verstappen ends drought as Russell suffers pain  - Bahrain GP Winners & Losers
excerpt:
Formula 1's improvised journey to Sepang produced a race weekend nobody will forget, for better or worse.

A software bug froze cars on the formation lap, George Russell's Mercedes died again, and Lando Norris speared into the Turn 1 gravel, yet somehow Max Verstappen still emerged with his hands on the trophy after 55 laps.

Sepang, drafted in at roughly 10 weeks' notice after the Bahrain Grand Prix was relocated amid security concerns, drew a record 261,000 fans across the weekend, even as transport chaos and a stalled start threatened to derail the show entirely.

Here are the winners and losers from a grand prix that was anything but conventional.

© Red Bull Content Pool

Winner - Max Verstappen

Verstappen converted a hectic opening, in which his power unit briefly refused to respond, into a maiden win for this year at Sepang, charging once his intermediates came to life after a poor start.

The Red Bull driver's call to switch tyres at the right moment proved decisive as conditions shifted lap by lap, and despite a late safety car to test his nerve, he was rarely troubled.

From the lows at the start of the season, Red Bull has delivered an RB22 of which it can be proud.

"It's a really nice one, after the year that we've had and the progression that we've made," Verstappen said. "I'm incredibly proud of everyone, and it's just super nice to win here.

"It was very hectic with a lot of different things in the start. No power, so you have to wait for the power to kick in. But then we made the right call with the intermediates, and after that, step by step, we moved our way forward."

© XPB Images

Winner - Malaysia

Handed the job of hosting F1 again in a matter of weeks, with 561 marshals mobilised and paddock fittings airlifted in from Bahrain, the local organisers delivered a record crowd and a circuit that reminded everyone why it was once a calendar fixture.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim even confirmed talks are underway with F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali about the track's future on the schedule.

Bahrain circuit chief Sheikh Salman Isa Al Khalifa was equally pleased with how the event turned out. "Over 260,000 fans came to witness the biggest event ever held at the Sepang International Circuit, and we are truly grateful to them for bringing their passion and energy," he said.

Yes, there were infrastructure issues outside the circuit, but at short notice, it was always going to be difficult to please all of the people, all the time. Overall, Sepang is a circuit that needs to be permanently back on the calendar.

© XPB Images

Winner - Fernando Alonso

It has been a horrid year for Aston Martin, but in Malaysia, the Silverstone-based squad delivered its best all-round performance of the campaign.

In qualifying, it managed to get both cars into Q2 for the first time this season, with Alonso lining up a year-high 12th, and team-mate Lance Stroll 14th.

Veteran Alonso then proved the pace over one lap was no fluke. He initially held his own in the tricky, changeable conditions, and once on slicks, although the AMR26 lacked a degree of performance, he still managed to deliver the team's best result this year with eighth.

© XPB Images

George Russell

Running third and seemingly on course for a decent haul of points, Russell suffered a suspected power unit failure during a late safety car period, forcing him to pull over on the main straight and retire. It capped a bruising weekend for the Mercedes driver.

After dominating in Baku the previous weekend, Russell could reasonably have hoped his campaign had turned a corner, but not a bit of it.

At no stage did he look comfortable around the Sepang track, culminating in his worst qualifying performance of the season with eighth. Although he was a rocket ship off the line in the wet conditions, it was clear he did not have the pace of team-mate Kimi Antonelli.

The retirement has seemingly dealt a fatal blow to his championship chances as he heads to Singapore this weekend now 84 points behind Antonelli.

© XPB Images

Lando Norris

Starting on the medium tyres in the wet conditions was a severe miscalculation that ensured his race got off to the worst possible start as he plummeted down the order, whilst those on inters all surged past.

A recovery followed as the race unfolded, but the damage had been done earlier, from which he never truly recovered, and a modest points haul was only ever on the cards.

Even that, however, was wrecked when he misjudged the cars ahead of him during a safety car period, forcing him to take evasive action that saw him drive over a kerb and the gravel before narrowly avoiding McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri.

Norris was summoned to the stewards post-race for alleged erratic driving, and was ultimately given his first reprimand of the season.

Formula 1

The sport's return to Sepang was overshadowed by an embarrassing technical failure that froze throttles on the formation lap.

The FIA later confirmed a software bug in the standard power unit controller triggered a lockdown mode, known as continuous offset, when cars slowed behind the safety car at Turn 9 and lost turbo boost pressure, cutting electrical deployment across the grid.

Technical delegate Nikolas Tombazis admitted the governing body had not had enough opportunity to stress-test the system. "We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked, because there's been very little wet running this year, and there was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in," he said.

Drivers across the grid, including Hamilton and Verstappen, were affected. Hamilton even had to stop and restart his car on the start-finish straight.

None of the drivers were happy, with Cadillac's Sergio Perez describing the situation as "unacceptable", and Norris saying that what unfolded was "horrible". It was not a good look for F1, the so-called pinnacle of the sport.

title: Jacques Villeneuve details clear difference between Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
1997 F1 champion Jacques Villeneuve has highlighted a key difference that exists between Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli.

Antonelli looks set to seal his maiden F1 title this year, as he currently holds an 84-point lead in the drivers' championship.

Last time out in Sepang, Antonelli ended the race in second place, behind Max Verstappen, who scored his first race victory of the season with Red Bull.

While it was a strong showing for Antonelli, it was not an error-free race; late on, he ran wide into the final corner and collected the bollard at pit entry, risking damage to his front wing.

Villeneuve noted that Verstappen is a much more polished driver at this stage, and believes Antonelli would be suffering championship-wise if Red Bull were on par with Mercedes.

"He [Verstappen] rarely makes mistakes," Villeneuve told Sky F1. "When he's on it, like he's been on this weekend, he's precise.

"You can see the difference with his teammate as well. He doesn't make the mistakes that Antonelli keeps making.

"So, in the championship balance, that would have weight. It's just a little bit too late in the season."

[Article continues below]

Villeneuve sends Antonelli warning over mistakes

Antonelli's championship hopes received a significant boost when team-mate George Russell was forced to retire from the Sepang race due to a power unit issue.

With just seven rounds and one sprint race remaining on the schedule, time is running out for Russell to claw back the deficit.

But Villeneuve warned that Antonelli could very easily suffer a non-finish in a similar fashion to Russell and see his advantage eaten into.

"He's controlling it, also because he is quicker than Russell in general," Villeneuve told Sky F1.

"Russell knows, so that will not make Russell quicker. It's tough.

"There are not a lot of races left, but there are some sprints, and Kimi can have some DNFs.

"He keeps making these tiny little mistakes, one of them will catch him out."

Navigating the treacherous mixed conditions and the late restart without incident, the Spaniard methodically picked his way through the order to finish eighth. It represented one of the drives of the day, and a reminder that experience still counts for plenty in changeable conditions at Sepang.

Kimi Antonelli - 8.5

Antonelli qualified a strong fourth and converted that into a brilliant runner-up finish, extending his title lead The Mercedes driver kept pace with Verstappen for large stretches before the Dutchman's tyre management proved decisive in clear air. Even so, finishing ahead of both Ferraris and the second Red Bull of Hadjar was a significant statement from the 20-year-old Italian.

Charles Leclerc - 8

Leclerc qualified fifth, a tenth and a half off his team-mate, and spent the race working his way into contention. Like Hamilton, he preserved his tyres through the tricky conditions and advanced during the closing laps to take fourth, giving Ferrari a double points haul to end a difficult weekend on a high note.

The bottom five

Gabriel Bortoleto - 5

Bortoleto qualified a respectable 10th for Audi but ruined his race with a Safety Car restart collision that tagged Carlos Sainz and sent both drivers tumbling down the order. The stewards handed him a 10-second penalty for causing the incident, and he eventually finished 18th. A promising Saturday undone entirely by a self-inflicted error at the restart.

Alex Albon - 5

Albon qualified a lowly 20th for Williams and his afternoon unravelled further from there. A delayed double-stack pit stop under the early Safety Car cost him further ground, and he was running 19th when a gearbox failure forced retirement on Lap 41. His stricken car then triggered the late Safety Car that compressed the field for the finish, denying him even a passive role in the shake-up.

Valtteri Bottas - 5

Bottas qualified 21st for Cadillac, already facing an uphill task in Malaysia's slippery early conditions. His race lasted only nine laps before he lost grip on slick tyres and speared into the gravel trap at Turn 13. A short and forgettable weekend for the Finn, with little to salvage from either session.

Sergio Perez - 5

Perez's weekend was compromised from the start, exiting in Q1 and lining up at the back of the grid. His opening stint on slick tyres in wet conditions left him on the back foot, and although he attempted to recover through a five-stop strategy, ill-timed Safety Car periods repeatedly neutralised his pace. He finished 19th, never truly in the fight.

Lando Norris - 4.5

Norris's weekend was a mess from the opening laps, when a gamble on slick medium tyres on a still-wet track left him exposed and sliding through the order. Worse followed late on, when he ran into the Turn 1 gravel avoiding a collision with Oscar Piastri after George Russell's retirement under the Safety Car. The FIA handed him a reprimand for erratic driving behind the Safety Car, citing low sun and reduced visibility as contributing factors. He salvaged two points in ninth, but it did little to soften a chastening afternoon for the McLaren driver.

title: Valtteri Bottas taking remarkable route to Singapore after ditching plane
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has begun his journey from Malaysia to Singapore on a bicycle, sharing the start of the ride on Instagram on Sunday night, hours after finishing last at the Bahrain Grand Prix at the Sepang International Circuit.

The Cadillac driver's Strava account showed he covered 56.6 kilometres from the circuit to Port Dickson, taking two hours and eight minutes to complete the leg.

It marks an unconventional way to get from race-to-race with Singapore following Malaysia directly on the 2026 calendar and the Marina Bay Street Circuit hosting round 17 this coming weekend.

Bottas is known as one of the paddock's most committed cyclists away from the cockpit.

The Finn has co-founded gravel races including FNLD GRVL in his home country and RADL GRVL in Australia, and this year qualified for the UCI Gravel World Championships through top-five age-category finishes in the UCI Gravel World Series.

His relationship with cycling extends to his personal life too, as he is dating Tiffany Cromwell, the Australian professional road and gravel rider.

The switch from Sepang to Marina Bay is itself one of the more demanding transitions on the calendar.

Freight for the two events must clear customs and cross the Malaysia-Singapore border within a tight window, while teams and drivers face a swift adjustment from daytime running in Malaysia to Singapore's night race, held under floodlights.

title: Max Verstappen survived nail in tyre during chaotic Bahrain GP in Malaysia
excerpt:
Max Verstappen cruised to a dominant victory in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, but things could have come unstuck thanks to a rogue nail.

Nothing appeared capable of stopping the Red Bull driver throughout the weekend at the Sepang International Circuit, though a sizeable piece of metal made a decent attempt at it.

The race was thrown into disarray after a botched start procedure forced drivers to be called back into the pits, with software updates required to eradicate a "bug" that caused the farcicial scenes on the initial formation lap.

And as Verstappen trundled down the pit lane behind the safety car, he picked up a nail in one of his tyres.

Once he had brought the RB22 to a halt, Verstappen radioed his team to report the issue.

"There's a nail in my tyre," the four-time F1 drivers' champion said.

Race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase immediately asked whether it was the front-left.

"Front-left," the 72-time grand prix winner confirmed.

The mechanics waiting trackside with cooling equipment had already spotted the nail themselves, given it was hardly difficult to miss.

Rules working in Verstappen's favour

The mechanics waiting trackside with cooling equipment had already spotted the nail themselves, given it was hardly difficult to miss.

With the regulations allowing for tyre changes during a red-flag neutralisation, a potentially disastrous scenario was negated.

Verstappen opted for a fresh, nail-free set of intermediates, while some of his rivals, less fortunately, went straight onto slick tyres for the restart.

A further safety car period then gave Verstappen the chance to switch from intermediates to slicks along with everyone else, setting him up for this comfortable victory.

title: F1 drivers shocked following bizarre problem that caused huge delay
excerpt:
It was a bizarre sight that was ultimately not a good look for Formula 1.

On the formation lap for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the pinnacle of motorsport was made to look like "the Lego race", as pointed out by seven-time F1 champion Lewis Hamilton after the event at the Sepang International Circuit had concluded.

That was with reference to last year's 'race' in Miami when the drivers clambered aboard near life-size F1 Lego cars ahead of the Miami Grand Prix, and had more fun over one lap than on many occasions in their own F1 machinery.

As the formation lap unfolded behind the safety car in Sepang, deployed following a thunderstorm and torrential downpour to test the track and get driver feedback on whether there should be a standing start, a number started touring remarkably slowly.

Sparked by polesitter Max Verstappen out front, others followed, including Hamilton, who eventually stopped on the start-finish straight where a reboot was effectively required to get his SF-26 moving again.

The FIA is to undertake a full review of the incident that led to a delay of over an hour, as the sporting body's Technical Department was forced to implement an updated software release due to "an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration" which " led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars".

Naturally, many drivers were shocked, confused, and unhappy with what unfolded.

Check out their comments below.

Max Verstappen - "These engines are so complicated, and a lot of software is implemented, and when there is something like this, that's the problem. What can you say? I mean, that's not what you want for the sport? Hopefully, there is a lesson learned."

Kimi Antonelli - "It was insane. At some point, we were five wide in the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on."

George Russell - "The power units are exceptionally complicated. The more complicated you make things, the more there is to go wrong. So that is obviously something we need to bear in mind for the future."

Lando Norris - "[It was] Horrible! It just proves that we shouldn't have any of that stuff, the electronic side, with what happened."

Pierre Gasly - "It was like the most chaotic formation lap I've had in my career, and with limited information. It was very strange."

Gabriel Bortoleto - "It's not great, is it? It's just a shame because maybe a wet race could have been interesting, but the issue happened, we had to fix it, and it took a lot of time."

Liam Lawson - "I had no radio; I knew I had no radio before I even pulled away for the formation lap. I was very stressed because there are a lot of procedures you have to do, especially in this year's car. I was like, 'I have no idea what's going on'. It was very confusing when all the cars were slowing down. I couldn't talk to the team; I didn't know if I was allowed to overtake or what."

Sergio Perez - "It felt like you were in a rental [go-] kart and you ran out of time. It's obviously not great what happened. I'm sure we will learn from it as a sport, but what happened is totally unacceptable for the sport."

Charles Leclerc - "I don't want to be so extreme with my words, but surely it's not good enough. We've been raising these issues, and I hope that we fix them. Unfortunately, I don't think there are any short-term solutions. These problems are the result of decisions made quite a long time ago, and changing that is going to take time."

Arvid Lindblad - "It was a bit weird. You're kind of like, 'What's what's going on here'. At one point I had no power; the pedal just didn't work. I've had it before in the sim, but the sim sometimes has weird stuff that happens. When you're in a real car, and you're pressing the throttle and the thing just doesn't move, it's a bit weird."

Ollie Bearman -" I was shocked! I didn't even know the FIA could control our throttle pedal [laughs]. But I got a glitch in my throttle pedal. That's a new experience in Formula 1. I don't think we were expecting that one."

title: McLaren set latest timeline for Gianpiero Lambiase arrival from Red Bull
excerpt:
McLaren announced earlier this year that it had signed Gianpiero Lambiase from Red Bull, stating he would join no later than 2028.

McLaren CEO Zak Brown has voiced hope that Gianpiero Lambiase will take up a working position within the team at some point next year.

Earlier this year, McLaren announced the signing of Lambiase, stating he would arrive at the team "no later than 2028".

It declared that he would take up the position of chief racing officer and report to team principal Andrea Stella.

However, this has been disputed by Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies, who stated that he believes Lambiase is joining McLaren to take on the team principal role.

Lambiase has served as Max Verstappen's race engineer since the Dutchman joined the team in 2016, with the two striking up one of the most successful partnerships seen in the sport.

But as the working relationship nears its end, Brown has delivered his latest ambition to see Lambiase at the team during 2027.

"I'm optimistic that we'll see him in papaya at some point next year," he told Sky F1.

[Article continues below]

Brown 'very excited' over McLaren future

McLaren has endured a challenging F1 campaign, with its form slipping of late as it has fallen behind in the pecking order after two wins in the mid-point of the season.

But as it seeks to get itself back in top form, Brown insisted McLaren is in a very healthy position when it comes to its entire racing operation, which will see it enter the Hypercar category in the World Endurance Championship next year.

"I'm very excited about everything that we've got going on at the factory, the men and women have been doing a great job," he said.

"We've made a lot of gains this year from what was a very tough start to the year, but I feel like we're on top of things now-ish.

"There's still a lot of work to do, the drivers are driving great, it's exciting times. We've got the World Endurance [Championship] going on, our IndyCar team.

"So it's good to have a papaya shirt to show up to work at the MTC every day."
